name: Australian Camp
tagline: A grassy ridge at 2,060 m, one hour's walk from the road
meta_description: Australian Camp guide: the 1–1.5 hour walk from Kande, sunrise on Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre, lodges, permits and the easy trek on to Dhampus.
summary: Australian Camp is a meadow on a forested ridge at about 2,060 m, north-west of Pokhara. From Kande on the Pokhara–Baglung road it is a 1–1.5 hour walk uphill, and the reward is one of the closest easy views of Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machhapuchhre. Stay overnight for sunset and sunrise.
intro: The camp takes its name, so the local story goes, from Australian trekking groups who pitched their tents on this open ridge in the 1970s and 80s. Today it is a broad, sloping lawn with a handful of lodges and a tented camp along its upper edge, surrounded by oak and rhododendron forest. It sits inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, but at 2,060 m it is low enough that altitude is not a concern for healthy travellers.

The view is the reason to come. Machhapuchhre seems close enough to touch from here, about 20 km to the north-east, with Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Mardi Himal and the Annapurna massif along the skyline, and the Lamjung Himal further east. In the evening the peaks turn orange and the lights of Pokhara come on in the valley to the south-east. In the morning the sun rises behind Machhapuchhre and lights the whole range.

Australian Camp is the easiest taste of the Annapurna foothills. Families, older travellers and honeymoon couples do it as an overnight trip from Pokhara, while trekkers pass through on the first day of the Mardi Himal trek or on the walk to Dhampus and Landruk. The trail from Kande is a steady stone staircase through forest, short enough for children from about six. Allow a full afternoon and the following morning; the drive back from Kande or Phedi to Lakeside takes under an hour.
facts: ≈ 25 km · 45–60 min drive to Kande + 1–1.5 h walk
Close views of Machhapuchhre and Annapurna South, easy overnight hike

highlights.title: Sunrise behind Machhapuchhre
highlights.text: At dawn the sun climbs from behind Machhapuchhre's twin summit, outlining it in gold before lighting Annapurna South and Hiunchuli. Unlike Sarangkot, there are no tour buses, and you watch from the lawn a few steps from your lodge door.

highlights.title: Sunset over the Pokhara valley
highlights.text: Late afternoon light paints the Annapurnas pink while the valley to the south fills with haze. As dark falls, the lights of Pokhara and Phewa Lake come on far below. Clear evenings from October to December are the most reliable.

highlights.title: The stone trail from Kande
highlights.text: The walk up from Kande at about 1,770 m climbs roughly 300 m in 1–1.5 hours on stone steps through oak and rhododendron forest. It is steady rather than steep and passes a few tea shops for rests.

highlights.title: Rhododendron forest in spring
highlights.text: From late February to April the forest around the camp and along the ridge to Pothana flowers red and pink with rhododendron, Nepal's national flower. It is one of the easiest places near Pokhara to see the bloom.

highlights.title: Walk on to Dhampus
highlights.text: From Australian Camp an easy trail continues east through forest and fields to Pothana at about 1,990 m, then down to the Gurung village of Dhampus. This makes a classic two-day loop back to Pokhara via Phedi.

how_to_reach.text: Drive from Pokhara north-west on the Pokhara–Baglung highway towards Naudanda for about 25 km to Kande (45–60 minutes by private car or taxi). Local buses to Baglung pass Kande but are slower. Your vehicle can collect you at Kande or, if you walk on to Dhampus, at Phedi.

From Kande, a stone trail climbs about 300 m through forest to Australian Camp in 1–1.5 hours. A guide is required for foreign trekkers under current Annapurna Conservation Area rules. From the camp, Pothana is about 1 hour east and Dhampus another 1–1.5 hours beyond.

where_to_stay: Several family-run lodges and a tented camp stand along the top of the meadow, most with rooms or tents facing the mountains. Rooms are simple, with twin beds, blankets and either shared or basic attached bathrooms; hot showers are often solar or gas-heated. Meals are dal bhat, noodles, pancakes and simple Indian and continental dishes. There are no hotels of 3-star standard here, so pack a warm layer and a sleeping bag liner in winter. We reserve the best available view rooms for our guests, and travellers who prefer more comfort can do the hike as a day trip and return to Pokhara.
tips: Start the walk from Kande by 2 pm so you reach the camp before the evening light show.
Carry a warm jacket and hat; December and January nights drop close to freezing at 2,060 m.
Bring your ACAP permit and TIMS card, which may be checked on the trail.
Leave heavy luggage in Pokhara and carry only an overnight daypack up the steps.
Pay for hot showers and phone charging in cash, as lodges charge small fees for both.

experiences.title: Sunrise on Annapurna South from Australian Camp
experiences.price_hint: Included in our Australian Camp trek
experiences.summary: Step out of your lodge at dawn onto the grassy ridge at 2,060 m as the sun rises behind Machhapuchhre and lights Annapurna South and Hiunchuli. Closer to the peaks than Sarangkot and without the crowds.
body: Sunrise at Australian Camp needs no drive and no climb: the lawn is the viewpoint, a few steps from your room. Get up about half an hour before sunrise, take a mug of tea from the lodge kitchen and find a spot on the slope. The sky behind Machhapuchhre brightens first, outlining the fishtail summit against orange light, then the sun appears and the snows of Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and the Annapurna massif turn from pink to white.

From here Machhapuchhre is only about 20 km away, so it looks far larger than from Pokhara, and you can pick out the ridges of Mardi Himal on its flank. Looking west, the forested hills roll away towards Dhampus and Kande; to the south, morning cloud often fills the Pokhara valley like a lake. Photographers will want a mid-range zoom of about 24–105 mm. Pothana's prayer flags and the trail to Dhampus are visible along the ridge to the east.

Clear sunrises are most reliable from October to December, when the air is dry. In February to April the light is softer and haze can appear, but rhododendrons flower in the forest around the camp. From June to September cloud usually hides the peaks. After breakfast, walk on to Pothana and Dhampus or return to Kande. Lodges serve breakfast from about 7 am, so you can watch the whole sunrise before eating and still set off on time.

faqs.q: Is the sunrise at Australian Camp better than Sarangkot?
faqs.a: It is closer to the mountains and much quieter, so many people prefer it. Machhapuchhre and Annapurna South look larger, and you watch from the lawn by your lodge without crowds. Sarangkot gives a wider panorama including Dhaulagiri and Phewa Lake and is reachable by car. Australian Camp needs an overnight stay.

faqs.q: How cold is Australian Camp at sunrise?
faqs.a: From December to February it can be around 0 to 3 °C before dawn, and frost is common on the grass. In October, November and March expect about 5–8 °C. Wear a down jacket, hat and gloves, and take a hot drink from the lodge. It warms quickly once the sun is up.

faqs.q: What camera lens do I need at Australian Camp?
faqs.a: A mid-range zoom of about 24–105 mm covers both the full range and close detail of Machhapuchhre. A wide lens helps capture the meadow and lodges in the foreground. A phone camera works well too. Carry a spare battery, since cold mornings drain batteries quickly.

experiences.title: Kande to Australian Camp hike
experiences.price_hint: Included in our Australian Camp trek
experiences.image_query: Kande Australian Camp trail stone steps
experiences.summary: The shortest way into the Annapurna foothills: a 1–1.5 hour climb of about 300 m on a stone staircase through oak and rhododendron forest from Kande on the Baglung road to the meadow of Australian Camp. Easy grade, suitable for families.
body: The drive from Pokhara to Kande takes 45–60 minutes on the Pokhara–Baglung highway, climbing past Hemja and the Tibetan settlement at Hyangja and up through terraced hills. Kande, at about 1,770 m, is a small roadside village with tea shops where the trail starts beside a signboard. Your guide checks permits here while you adjust your daypack and walking sticks. The road is paved all the way, and the drive itself gives early views of Machhapuchhre above the terraces.

The trail climbs on well-laid stone steps through forest of oak, chestnut and rhododendron, with occasional clearings that open views back over the Kaski hills. The gradient is steady and a comfortable pace with rests takes about 1–1.5 hours, gaining roughly 300 m. Midway there are small tea shops selling soft drinks and biscuits. Langur monkeys and forest birds such as laughingthrushes and barbets are often heard in the trees.

The forest opens suddenly onto the lawn of Australian Camp, and the mountains appear all at once. Plan to arrive in the mid-afternoon to settle into the lodge before sunset. The walk back down to Kande takes about 45 minutes; the alternative is to continue to Dhampus the next day. Wear proper walking shoes, as the steps can be slippery in damp weather. In October and November the camp fills by late afternoon, so an earlier start also secures the better view rooms.

faqs.q: How difficult is the walk to Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Easy to moderate. It is 1–1.5 hours uphill on stone steps from Kande, gaining about 300 m, with tea shops to rest at along the way. Children from about six and active seniors manage it at a slow pace. People with knee problems should use walking poles, especially coming down.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Yes. Australian Camp lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so you need an ACAP entry permit, and foreign trekkers also need a TIMS card and, under rules introduced in 2023, a licensed guide. SAARC nationals pay a lower ACAP fee. We arrange these for you. Check current status before you travel, as rules change.

faqs.q: Can I do Australian Camp as a day hike from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Yes. Leave Pokhara by 7 am, walk up from Kande in 1–1.5 hours, spend an hour or two on the ridge and walk down to Kande or on to Dhampus and Phedi in the afternoon, back in Pokhara by evening. Mountain views are usually clearer in the morning, but an overnight gives sunset and sunrise.

experiences.title: Birding in the forests around Australian Camp
experiences.summary: Walk slowly with a birding guide through the oak and rhododendron forest between Australian Camp and Pothana, looking for laughingthrushes, sunbirds, minivets, woodpeckers and, with luck, the Himalayan monal's lowland cousins, the kalij pheasant. Spring flowers add colour.
body: The ridge between Kande, Australian Camp and Pothana carries mixed forest of oak, chestnut, alder and rhododendron between about 1,800 and 2,100 m, a rich band for Himalayan birds. Set out at first light, when birds are most active, and walk slowly along the main trail east towards Pothana and the side paths that run through the trees. The first two hours after sunrise are the most productive, before the mixed flocks disperse and trekkers start to pass.

Common sightings include white-throated and rufous-chinned laughingthrushes, great barbets, scarlet minivets, Himalayan bulbuls, green-tailed sunbirds feeding on rhododendron flowers and several woodpeckers. Kalij pheasants sometimes cross the trail, and raptors such as Himalayan griffons, black eagles and steppe eagles in winter soar over the ridge. A good local guide knows the calls and can find mixed flocks in the canopy. Spring also brings cuckoos calling from the ridge, and in winter flocks of finches feed in the fields near Pothana.

Spring, from March to May, is the best season, with breeding plumage, song and flowering rhododendrons. October to December is also good, with clear views and winter visitors. Bring binoculars and a field guide or app, wear muted colours and keep voices low. This walk can be fitted into the morning of the Australian Camp to Dhampus trek. Our guide can bring a spotting scope on request, and lodges at Australian Camp serve early tea for birders setting out at dawn.

faqs.q: What birds can I see near Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Expect laughingthrushes, great barbets, scarlet minivets, sunbirds, bulbuls, tits, woodpeckers and possibly kalij pheasant, with raptors such as Himalayan griffons and black eagles overhead. Spring brings breeding songbirds and winter brings migrant raptors. A local birding guide will greatly increase the number of species you see.

faqs.q: When is the best time for birdwatching near Pokhara?
faqs.a: March to May is best in the foothill forests, when birds are breeding and singing and rhododendrons flower. October to February is good for raptors and wetland birds around Phewa, Begnas and Rupa lakes. Early mornings are always more productive than afternoons.

faqs.q: Do I need special equipment for birding at Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Binoculars of 8x or 10x magnification are the main need, plus a field guide to the birds of Nepal or a birding app. Wear muted clothing and comfortable walking shoes. A camera with a 300 mm or longer lens helps for photography, as many birds stay high in the canopy.

faqs.q: How do I get to Australian Camp from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Drive about 25 km north-west on the Pokhara–Baglung highway to Kande, 45–60 minutes by car, then walk 1–1.5 hours uphill on a stone trail to the camp. Alternatively, start at Phedi and walk via Dhampus and Pothana, about 4 hours. Most people go up from Kande and come down via Dhampus.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Australian Camp?
faqs.a: About 2,060 m, roughly 1,240 m higher than Pokhara Lakeside and 300 m above the trailhead at Kande. This is well below the height where altitude sickness is usually a concern, so it suits families and seniors in normal health. Nights are cold in winter.

faqs.q: Is Australian Camp good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. The 1–1.5 hour walk from Kande is short and steady, the meadow is safe for children to play on and the overnight in a lodge with mountain views is a real adventure for them. Bring warm clothes and snacks. Children from about six usually walk it on their own.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Yes. Several simple lodges and a tented camp stand along the meadow, with twin rooms, basic bathrooms and dal bhat meals. Book ahead in October and November. Facilities are basic but the setting is the point: sunset and sunrise over the Annapurnas from your doorstep.

faqs.q: What can I see from Australian Camp?
faqs.a: On clear days Machhapuchhre (6,993 m), Annapurna South (7,219 m), Hiunchuli, Mardi Himal, the Annapurna massif and Lamjung Himal, with the Pokhara valley to the south-east. Views are clearest at sunrise and sunset from October to December. Bring binoculars to pick out the ice ridges.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Australian Camp?
faqs.a: October to December has the clearest skies. February to April adds rhododendron flowers in the forest, though haze increases by April. June to September is the monsoon, with cloud, rain and leeches on the trail, and is best avoided. January is clear but cold at night.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory for Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Under rules introduced by Nepal in 2023, foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas, including the Annapurna Conservation Area, must trek with a licensed guide. Enforcement and exemptions, including for Indian nationals, have varied, so check current status before you travel. Our treks always include a licensed guide.

faqs.q: How much does the Australian Camp trek cost?
faqs.a: A guided two-night trek from Pokhara including transport, permits, guide and lodge meals costs roughly US$ 180–260 or ₹15,000–22,000 per person depending on group size. Doing it independently costs less but foreign trekkers need a licensed guide. Our package price includes all of these.

faqs.q: Can I see Australian Camp and Dhampus in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes, this is the classic route. Walk up from Kande to Australian Camp on day one, continue east through forest to Pothana and down to Dhampus on day two, and descend to Phedi and drive back to Pokhara on the morning of day three. Each walking day is 1.5–3 hours.
